body_text: View All News Community Financial System, Inc. Announces Increase to Its Quarterly Dividend Resulting in Its 34th Consecutive Year of Dividend Increases July 22, 2026 Download (opens in new window) SYRACUSE, N.Y.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Community Financial System, Inc. (NYSE: CBU) (the “Company”) announced that it has declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.49 per share on its common stock, which represents a $0.02, or 4.26%, increase and an annualized yield of 2.89% based on the closing share price of $67.82 on July 21, 2026. The dividend will be payable on October 13, 2026 to Shareholders of record as of September 15, 2026. President and Chief Executive Officer, Dimitar Karaivanov, commented, “Given the Company’s strong performance in 2026, the Board of Directors is pleased to provide its Shareholders with a larger increase to the dividend this year, and has raised the quarterly dividend from $0.47 per share of common stock to a quarterly dividend of $0.49 per share of common stock. This increase emphasizes our commitment to sustained shareholder returns. Our annual dividend increases over the last 34 years are supported by our strong balance sheet and cash flow generation that provide us with flexibility to return cash to our Shareholders while investing in our long-term future.” About Community Financial System, Inc. Community Financial System, Inc. is a diversified financial services company that is focused on four main business lines – banking services, employee benefit services, insurance services and wealth management services. Its banking subsidiary, Community Bank, N.A., is among the country’s 100 largest banking institutions with over $17 billion in assets and operates approximately 200 customer facilities across Upstate New York, Northeastern Pennsylvania, Vermont, Western Massachusetts and Southern New Hampshire. The Company’s Benefit Plans Administrative Services, Inc. subsidiary is a leading provider of employee benefits administration, trust services, collective investment fund administration, and actuarial consulting services to customers on a national scale. The Company’s OneGroup NY, Inc. subsidiary is a top 68 U.S. insurance agency. The Company also offers comprehensive financial planning, trust administration and wealth management services through its Nottingham Financial Group operating unit. The Company is listed on the New York Stock Exchange and the Company’s stock trades under the symbol CBU. For more information about the Company and each of its four main business lines visit https://ir.cfsi.com . title: Considerations when buying managed security services
summary: Access to the best cybersecurity talent, products and intelligence can be expensive and difficult to manage for a single enterprise on its own. Managed security service providers (MSSPs), on the other hand, offer the scale and expertise to provide these capabilities in a cost-effective and highly skilled way.
body_text: The trend for organizations of all shapes and sizes in buying managed security services continues to increase, and we’re seeing a rise in interest from all sectors. Is it any wonder? Access to the best cybersecurity talent, products and intelligence can be expensive and difficult to manage for a single enterprise on its own. Managed security service providers (MSSPs), on the other hand, offer the scale and expertise to provide these capabilities in a cost-effective and highly skilled way. But with so many managed security service providers out there, how do you choose the right one for you? Here are four key areas where you can look for deep expertise and reference-ability: Managed detection and response (MDR) and hunting – Do they provide skilled expertise or are they just deploying tools and letting the machine do the hunting? True cyber threat intelligence analysts – Does their threat intelligence capability just give you a third-party feed, or are they actually doing the research? Holistic contextual security – Do they truly understand your business and the risks associated with it? Efficiency and innovation – Do they, for example, use machine learning for scale and additional levels of security? The Managed Security Forum Buyers’ Guide to UK Managed Security , a report to which CGI contributed, explores these topics in more detail. (A fast and simple registration is needed to download this report.) The report maps services into basic, core, advanced and complementary categories, and offers further advice on what to look for from MSSPs. It also shows what services are being commoditized and where talent is most valued, allowing chief information security officers (CISOs) and business owners to work out what they should deliver in-house, and where it makes sense to bring in an outside expert. Other findings from the report include: Talent remains the top priority for 21% of MSSPs, followed by MDR and artificial intelligence (11% each). Security architects are the most difficult roles to fill for 28% of companies, followed by threat intel specialists (22%), threat hunters and senior analysts (16% each). Just 30% of MSSPs are investing in an internal data science function. Managed security is evolving from a compliance “tick–box” exercise into a fully formed and crucial part of enterprise architecture and national defense activities. It’s important that organizations get cybersecurity right, or the consequences can be devastating. CGI has invested heavily in our MSSP credentials and capabilities, working closely with international security associations and standards bodies. For information on how we help clients manage their security needs to operate with confidence, please visit our managed security services page , or contact me .

title: Who’s Training Tomorrow’s Experts?
summary: Agentic AI automates entry-level work first. Training talent in the age of AI means redesigning apprenticeship and hiring before the pipeline dries up.
body_text: Industries Financial Services contributors Terry Peters Managing Director, Brand Experience share article Share Share July 16, 2026 • 5 Min Read If you're a CHRO who's been asked to produce a 2030 workforce strategy, you've already experienced the problem: an honest version of that document can't really be built. That’s because any role map or headcount forecast you produce will be outdated before it's presented. The problem isn’t that the board's question is unreasonable; it’s that it’s being asked in the wrong form. Every senior person currently working got there the same way. They did the entry-level work, they made mistakes, and someone corrected them. Over years, that accumulation of small failures and course corrections became the pattern recognition that makes a person senior. It’s not a glamorous process and it doesn’t show up on a resume, but it’s the only mechanism anyone has ever found for producing people who actually know what they’re doing. The evidence is already on Wall Street On Wall Street, the conversation has become unusually candid. Goldman Sachs President John Waldron has described traditional bank operations as a “ human assembly line ” ready for automation. Citigroup’s Jane Fraser has told staff: “ some roles will change , new ones will emerge and others will no longer be required.” What makes that candor worth paying attention to is the paradox sitting beneath it. According to QuantumBlack, McKinsey’s AI consulting arm, banks are shrinking junior analyst classes by as much as two-thirds. Those same junior cohorts supply roughly 62% of the banks’ own AI talent. The rationale for cutting is hard to argue with in the short term. If a senior analyst plus an AI tool can produce the output of three juniors, the economic case for hiring trainees weakens considerably. The concern is that in seven years there may be no directors, because nobody learned how to become one. Automating entry-level work doesn’t eliminate the need for senior judgment. It eliminates the path to it. The cohort entering the workforce now may be the last to be trained in anything resembling the traditional way. They’ll arrive expecting the apprenticeship that built every senior before them and instead find themselves supervising AI systems in roles designed for productivity, not development. That’s a problem with a long fuse. The organization looks fine. Output is up. Efficiency metrics are strong. But the internal capacity to develop the next generation of senior people, the people who can catch what agents miss, who can read a situation the model wasn’t trained on, who can decide which problems are actually worth solving, is quietly eroding. And it likely won’t announce itself until it’s expensive to fix. Apprenticeship has to be engineered deliberately The response most organizations reach for is a training program, but judgment doesn’t form in a classroom. It forms through experience. An alternative looks something like this: Resist the urge to measure early career professionals by output. Output is what agents are for. Junior professionals are for judgment formation, and judgment forms slowly. If the metric is volume of work cleared, you’re measuring the wrong thing and incentivizing the wrong behavior. Make critiquing agent output part of the job description. Not approving it. Critiquing it. Grade on the quality of the critique: did this person find what was wrong, name why it was wrong, and redirect correctly? A junior who gets good at catching what agents miss is developing exactly the pattern recognition the organization needs. Don’t let junior employees specialize too early. Judgment develops by seeing many kinds of decisions, not repeating the same one. Rotate them through different AI-assisted workflows so they learn to recognize different patterns of failure. Redesigning apprenticeship also means redesigning hiring. If AI increasingly performs the execution, hiring for execution no longer makes much sense. The job description has to change before the hiring does In today’s world, existing recruitment systems are built around skills. Resumes list skills. Job descriptions require skills. Interviews test skills. However, skills are increasingly what agents do well. This begs and obvious question: If we’re not hiring for execution anymore, what are we hiring for? The answer? We’re hiring for the kind of capabilities AI doesn’t develop naturally: Judgment is the ability to decide what’s worth doing, not just execute what’s been assigned. An AI wealth management agent can identify every portfolio that should be rebalanced. What it can’t recognize is a client who just lost a spouse shouldn’t receive an automated investment recommendation this week, regardless of what the model suggests. The recommendation isn’t technically wrong, but it’s wrong for the moment. Taste is the ability to recognize when something’s wrong before you can explain why. In an interview with a recruiter, AI-generated summary will accurately capture every answer the candidate gave but miss the quality that made that candidate memorable. Nothing in the summary is technically wrong. It’s simply missing what mattered most. Direction is the ability to instruct, supervise, and redirect non-human collaborators. An agent given a vague brief will produce a confident answer to the wrong question. The person who can write a precise brief, review the output against intent rather than against instructions, and redirect without starting over is doing something genuinely difficult. None of these capabilities appear on a traditional job description. But they’re increasingly the qualities that determine whether someone can become an expert in an AI-first organization. Human-Centered Design The organizations that will thrive tomorrow won’t be the ones that automate the most work. They’ll be the ones that deliberately redesign how expertise is built. Don’t stop hiring juniors. Just hire them for different reasons. If your junior roles no longer produce the judgment your future leaders will need, that’s a workforce design challenge, not a hiring one. See how RGP applies human-centered design to workforce transformation. Research & Insights You can’t hire for judgment until you understand what good judgment looks like inside your organization. That requires more than a competency model. It requires observing how experienced people actually make difficult decisions. That’s where research begins. Explore RGP’s Research & Insights approach. (“Chaince Digital” or the “Company”) (Nasdaq: CD) (formerly Mercurity Fintech Holding Inc.), a provider of tokenization solutions and digital-asset capital markets infrastructure, today announced that it continues to be included in the Russell 2000® Index for a second consecutive year in connection with the June 2026 Russell US Indexes reconstitution. The reconstituted indexes took effect after the close of U.S. equity markets on Friday, June 26, 2026, with trading in the newly reconstituted indexes commencing at the market open on Monday, June 29, 2026. The Russell 2000® Index is one of the most widely followed benchmarks for U.S. small-cap equities. The Company first joined the Russell 2000® Index at the June 2025 reconstitution, and its continued membership reflects the application of FTSE Russell’s objective, rules-based reconstitution methodology, which uses market-capitalization rankings, current index membership and other eligibility criteria. As a constituent of the Russell 2000® Index, Chaince Digital is also included in the broad-market Russell 3000® Index. FTSE Russell applies a rules-based style methodology to determine the relative growth and value weights of Russell 2000® constituents. The June 2026 reconstitution was the first cycle under FTSE Russell’s return to a semi-annual reconstitution schedule, under which the Russell US Indexes will now be rebalanced twice each year, in June and December. According to FTSE Russell, approximately US$12.2 trillion in assets are benchmarked to or invested in products based on the Russell US Indexes. title: FedRAMP EHR Status: What “Ready, In Process, Authorized, Moderate, and High Actually Mean
summary: Is a FedRAMP EHR required for government agencies? Yes for cloud systems handling federal health data — here’s the FISMA/FedRAMP policy chain, plainly explained
body_text: A FedRAMP status is really two separate pieces of information, glued together. One tells you how far along a platform is in getting approved. The other tells you what kind of data it’s allowed to touch. Read them apart, and any status — no matter how it’s worded — becomes easy to decode. What “FedRAMP status” actually means When someone says a product is “FedRAMP Authorized” or “FedRAMP Moderate,” they’re actually answering two different questions at once: Where is it in the approval process? (Ready, In Process, or Authorized) What data is it cleared to handle? (Moderate or High) Vendors often mash both into a single phrase — “FedRAMP Moderate In Process!” — and it can sound like a finished credential. It isn’t. Once you know to split the claim into its two parts, reading any FedRAMP status becomes significantlyless confusing. Part 1: Where is it in the approval process? Every platform moves through the same three stages, in the same order: Ready — An independent assessor has checked the platform’s security setup. It’s a real step, but no agency has approved it yet, and no risk has been accepted. In Process — The vendor is actively working with an agency toward approval. This shows momentum, not clearance. Some products stay “In Process for years. Some never finish. Authorized — The review is complete, and an agency has signed off. The platform holds an Authority to Operate (ATO). This is the only stage where a system can legally handle federal data. Think of it as a lifecycle, not a label. A platform can only be at one stage at a time, and only the last stage actually means anything is allowed to operate. Part 2: What data is it cleared to handle? This part has nothing to do with how far along a vendor is — it’s set by federal rules ( FIPS 199 ), based on how bad a breach would be: Moderate (~325 security controls) — covers data where a breach would cause serious harm. Most federal health data falls here. High (400+ controls) — covers data where a breach would be severe or even catastrophic. A lot of federal health information falls here too. Think of it as a ceiling, not a score. A platform authorized at Moderate cannot take on High-level data, no matter how solid its authorization otherwise is. If your agency’s data is categorized as High, you need a High-authorized platform. No exceptions. Putting the two parts together Once you can read both parts separately, combining them is simple. Ask one question about any vendor claim: “Authorized — at what level — by whom?” Only one combination actually clears a platform for federal use: Authorized, at the level your data requires. Everything short of that — Ready, In Process, or Authorized-but-at-the-wrong-level — is a work in progress, not a green light. How to read a real FedRAMP Marketplace listing With the two parts in mind, checking a real listing takes about thirty seconds. Look up the vendor and check three fields, in this order: Status — Ready, In Process, or Authorized Impact level — Li-SaaS, Low, Moderate, or High Authorizing agency — who actually approved it Then double-check you’re looking at the right product. Sometimes a listing covers a different edition of the software, or just the hosting layer underneath it — not the actual application. One thing worth knowing: a platform can hold a real ATO without ever showing up on the Marketplace. That’s not automatically a red flag — it just means you’ll need to verify it a different way. More on that here: FedRAMP Marketplace listing vs. agency ATO → Common mistakes when reading a status Treating “In Process” as good enough. It signals effort, not clearance. No agency has accepted the risk yet. Assuming a higher impact level is always better. It’s not a quality score — it’s a match to your data’s sensitivity. What matters is whether it meets your requirement. Stopping at the headline claim. “FedRAMP Moderate In Process” reads like a credential but is really two half-finished facts stacked together. Not checking who actually authorized it. An ATO from one agency doesn’t automatically mean every agency will accept it — though OMB policy pushes agencies to lean on existing authorizations rather than starting over. A quick heads-up: the labels are changing in 2026 FedRAMP is rolling out new terminology . “Authorized” is becoming “FedRAMP Certified,” and the old impact levels (Low, Moderate, High) are being replaced with class letters, A through D. The underlying security requirements haven’t changed — just the name you’ll see on listings and vendor sites going forward. Here’s how the classes stack up, from lowest assurance to highest: Class A — the lightest tier, meant as an on-ramp for cloud providers entering the federal market. It asks for less upfront documentation and lighter ongoing reporting. It’s a starting point, not a destination — vendors are expected to move up to Class B, C, or D as they take on more federal work. Class B and Class C — middle tiers for services with progressively more federal use and more sensitive data, with reporting and monitoring requirements that scale up accordingly. Class D — the highest tier. It replaces what used to be called “High,” and it’s reserved for mission-critical services where a breach could cripple agency operations or cause catastrophic harm. It requires the largest investment in both obtaining and maintaining certification. What “FedRAMP 20x Class A” means: as of today, FedRAMP has retired its old “Ready” status as the entry point for new vendors. “ FedRAMP 20x ” is the name of FedRAMP’s modernized certification program, and “Class A” is the new, lighter-weight starting certification within it — open to providers with an existing SOC 2 Type II audit who want a faster way into the federal market. It sits at the bottom of the new scale, roughly where “Ready” used to sit, not where “Authorized” did. What’s the highest certification for a FedRAMP EHR ? Class D — the same tier previously called “High.” Right now, Class D is only available through FedRAMP’s traditional agency-sponsored path (Rev5); a Class D option within the newer 20x program is expected to be piloted in late 2026 and formally available in early 2027. For an EHR or telehealth platform handling sensitive federal health data, a Class D (High) authorization is the top of the scale — the same bar VSee’s ATO is assessed against. FAQs What does “FedRAMP status” mean? It’s shorthand for two things at once: how far along a platform is in the approval process (Ready, In Process, Authorized), and what level of data it’s cleared to handle (Moderate or High). What does “FedRAMP In Process” mean? It means a vendor is actively working toward approval but hasn’t gotten it yet. No agency has accepted the risk, so the platform isn’t cleared for federal data. Can I use a platform that’s “In Process”? No. Only a completed authorization — at the impact level your data needs — clears a platform for federal use. Is FedRAMP Ready the same as FedRAMP Authorized? No. Ready just means a platform passed an initial security check. It hasn’t gone through full agency review, so it isn’t cleared to handle federal data yet. What does “FedRAMP Certified” mean? It’s FedRAMP’s newer name for what used to be called “Authorized.” Same requirement, new label. High-level (“Class D”) certification still means the toughest standard on the books. How long does it take to go from In Process to Authorized? It varies a lot by agency and platform complexity — anywhere from several months to a couple of years. There’s no fixed timeline, which is exactly why “In Process” alone doesn’t tell you much. Does an Authorized status ever expire? Authorized platforms have to go through continuous monitoring to keep their status current. It isn’t a one-time stamp — agencies expect ongoing proof the security posture holds up. What does “FedRAMP High” mean? FedRAMP High is the most stringent impact level (400+ NIST 800-53 controls), reserved for the government’s most sensitive unclassified data, including health information used in federal programs. What’s the difference between FedRAMP Moderate and High? It comes down to data sensitivity. Moderate covers serious-impact data (~325 controls). High covers the most sensitive data (400+ controls) — including a lot of federal health information. A Moderate platform can’t take on High-level work. What is an Authority to Operate (ATO)? An ATO is the formal approval a federal agency issues before a system goes live, certifying its security risk has been assessed and accepted. A FedRAMP High ATO means it was assessed against the FedRAMP High baseline. Which EHRs have a FedRAMP High ATO? Very few. VSee holds a FedRAMP High ATO issued by HHS ASPR; most others are Moderate, In Process, single-agency, or not FedRAMP. See the comparison → How do I verify a vendor’s FedRAMP status? Check the FedRAMP Marketplace ; if a vendor isn’t listed, request its ATO letter, impact level, authorizing agency, and System Security Plan — and confirm it’s the platform’s own ATO, not just its hosting. How long and how expensive is a FedRAMP authorization? Typically 12–18 months plus significant cost and staffing (several hundred thousand to a few million) — which is why deploying a platform that already holds a FedRAMP authorization removes the biggest time and risk from an agency’s project. What is the FedRAMP authorization process? A platform is assessed against the FedRAMP control baseline by an accredited third-party assessor, and a federal agency reviews the results and issues an ATO. The full path follows the NIST Risk Management Framework: Categorize the data’s impact level (Low / Moderate / High) Secure a federal agency sponsor Implement controls (typically on a FedRAMP-authorized cloud) Document them in a System Security Plan (SSP) Independent 3PAO (third-party assessment organization) assessment Remediate findings (tracked in a POA&M or Plan of Action & Milestones) Agency issues the ATO Maintain it through continuous monitoring Because this is long and demanding, deploying a platform that has already completed it removes most of that burden from your agency. Where VSee stands VSee holds a completed authorization at the highest level: a FedRAMP High ATO issued by HHS ASPR. title: Newell Brands Leaders Return from Cannes Lions with a Focus on AI, Growth and the Future of Marketing
body_text: Newell Brands Leaders Return from Cannes Lions with a Focus on AI, Growth and the Future of Marketing Share this story LINK COPIED TO YOUR CLIPBOARD Jul 15, 2026 Newell Brands Leaders Share Insights from Cannes Lions 2026 The Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity has evolved far beyond an awards show. Each year, the event brings together the world's leading marketers, media companies, technology platforms and creative organizations to explore the ideas shaping the future of brand building. This year, Newell Brands leaders joined those conversations with a focus on the trends and partnerships that will help drive the company's continued marketing transformation. Throughout the week, Chief Marketing Officer Nick Hammitt and Global Head of Media & Partnerships James Clarke met with strategic partners across the media, retail and technology landscape while participating in industry discussions centered on artificial intelligence, commerce media, measurement and the evolving consumer journey. Strengthening Strategic Partnerships As consumer behavior continues to evolve, collaboration across the marketing ecosystem has become increasingly important. During Cannes, Newell leaders met with partners including Amazon Ads, Walmart Connect, Reddit, Spotify, Pinterest, Google & YouTube, agencies and industry organizations to discuss emerging opportunities in retail media, AI-enabled advertising, audience measurement and commerce. These conversations reinforced the importance of building integrated partnerships that connect brand storytelling with measurable business outcomes across Newell's diverse portfolio of consumer brands. Exploring the Future of Marketing In addition to partner meetings, Newell leaders participated in sessions featuring some of the industry's foremost voices on marketing effectiveness, creativity and artificial intelligence. Discussions throughout the festival highlighted several themes that are shaping the future of marketing: Using AI to enhance creativity and streamline content production Advancing retail media and commerce as key growth drivers Improving measurement across increasingly complex consumer journeys Building brands through integrated, consumer-centric experiences rather than channel-specific thinking Creating marketing organizations that can adapt more quickly to changing technologies and behaviors These themes closely align with Newell's ongoing efforts to modernize its marketing capabilities and deliver stronger experiences for consumers. Sharing Newell's Perspective Beyond attending industry sessions and partner meetings, Newell leaders contributed to conversations shaping the future of marketing through interviews, panels and executive forums. Nick participated in executive discussions with industry leaders and marketers throughout the week, including appearances on the CPG Guys podcast and at the Harris Poll Content Studio. He also joined invitation-only executive roundtables and marketer forums focused on topics ranging from marketing effectiveness and brand growth to the role of AI in modern marketing. James also represented Newell on stage at the Brand Innovators Marketing Leadership Summit, joining fellow marketing leaders to discuss how brands can navigate an increasingly interconnected marketing ecosystem. During the festival, he also spoke with Ad Age during Xumo's "2-Minute Power Play: FAST, Unfiltered" series, sharing his perspective on the growing role of free ad-supported streaming television (FAST) as both a brand-building and performance marketing channel. Reflecting on the week, James noted that the most valuable moments often happened outside the formal sessions. "I've been thinking less about the sessions and more about the conversations." He also highlighted a theme that resonated throughout the festival: "Consumers don't experience channels. They experience brands." That idea echoed many of the discussions Newell leaders participated in throughout the week. As consumers move seamlessly between retailers, creators, social platforms, search and increasingly AI-powered experiences, the opportunity for marketers lies not in optimizing individual channels, but in creating connected brand experiences that drive sustainable growth. Building for What's Next The conversations at Cannes reinforced themes central to Newell’s broader marketing transformation, including the role of AI in helping teams create content with greater speed and scale. That work was also reflected in Adobe’s Cannes activation, where visuals from Newell’s collaborations with Adobe at Summit and MAX were featured in a broader video highlighting Adobe partners. Together, the week’s discussions and partnerships underscored a clear theme: the future of marketing will depend on how effectively organizations connect creativity, data, technology and agility. As Newell continues to invest in modern marketing capabilities, the insights and relationships developed during Cannes Lions will help inform future innovation and strengthen the company's ability to build brands that connect with consumers around the world. title: How to Choose the Best Payroll Provider With HR, Benefits, and Onboarding in 2026
summary: Once a company averages 50 full-time-equivalent employees in a calendar year, it becomes an Applicable Large Employer under the ACA and takes on new health-coverage reporting duties (IRS, checked July 10, 2026). That threshold is one reason payroll, HR, benefits,…
body_text: Once a company averages 50 full-time-equivalent employees in a calendar year, it becomes an Applicable Large Employer under the ACA and takes on new health-coverage reporting duties (IRS, checked July 10, 2026). That threshold is one reason payroll, HR, benefits, and onboarding decisions carry real stakes, and why this guide evaluates nine platforms, Asure included, on the same six criteria. The Decision You're Actually Making This Year You already know you want payroll, HR, benefits, and onboarding running through one system instead of three logins and a spreadsheet reconciling them. The harder question is who operates that system day to day, your own team, or someone else's. That choice sits underneath every provider on this list, even when the marketing doesn't say so. Some platforms assume your team will self-serve every workflow. Others, structured as a PEO, ask you to become a co-employer to get help running payroll and HR. AsureCentral and AsureWorks approach it differently. AsureCentral is Asure's self-service platform for running payroll, HR, benefits, time tracking, and onboarding in one login. AsureWorks is Asure's managed-service alternative, where Asure specialists handle the day-to-day execution on that same platform. There is no co-employment in AsureWorks, you remain the employer of record, and you keep your own choice of benefits, broker, and retirement partners. That makes Asure, through either AsureCentral or AsureWorks, one legitimate path to weigh alongside the eight other platforms this guide covers next, not an afterthought once everything else has been ruled out. Key Benchmarks at a Glance Cross 50 full-time-equivalent employees, and ACA Applicable Large Employer reporting duties begin under the employer shared responsibility rules (IRS, checked July 10, 2026). Publish three per-employee-per-month pricing tiers, Core at $10, Pro at $17, and Elite at $25, with a flat $250 monthly minimum for companies of 25 or fewer employees (BambooHR, accessed July 10, 2026). Payroll itself is sold as a separate, unpriced add-on, and a 15 percent discount applies when bundling payroll with benefits administration for US-based employees. Extend payroll processing to more than 140 countries and territories through ADP's Global Payroll add-on, which integrates with Workforce Now for businesses with international staff (ADP, accessed July 10, 2026). That figure describes the global-payroll integration, not a standalone Workforce Now specification. Require a sales conversation for pricing, with no public per-employee rate listed on Paycor's own pricing page (Paycor, accessed July 10, 2026). Leave G2 or Capterra ratings, review counts, benefits-carrier counts, and implementation-time benchmarks unconfirmed at a primary source for Gusto, ADP, Paycor, Rippling, BambooHR, Paylocity, Namely, and Justworks as of this review. This guide states that gap directly rather than estimating a number. What All in One Means and How These Platforms Were Evaluated For this guide, an all-in-one payroll provider is one where payroll processing, core HR records, benefits administration, and employee onboarding automation all run inside a single login, rather than through a separate onboarding tool or a benefits broker portal that requires its own credentials and a manual data sync between systems. Nine platforms are evaluated here, AsureCentral and AsureWorks together as one entry, plus Gusto, ADP Workforce Now, Paycor, Rippling, BambooHR, Paylocity, Namely, and Justworks, against six criteria: Payroll accuracy and compliance: tax filing handling, multi-state support, and compliance responsiveness. HR module depth: employee records, org management, and reporting capability. Benefits carrier integrations: breadth of benefits administration, self-service enrollment, and ACA compliance support. Onboarding automation: e-signature, new-hire task workflows, and day-one readiness. Pricing transparency: whether per-employee pricing is public or requires a sales call. Implementation time: how long it takes to get payroll live, where a source exists. Each criterion is rated Strong, Moderate, Limited, or Not publicly disclosed. These labels are qualitative judgments grounded in the public evidence available at the time of writing, not a precise numeric formula, and every "Not publicly disclosed" label reflects an honest gap in available data rather than an estimate. Asure's HR Module Depth is rated Moderate here specifically for core HR workflow depth (performance management, learning, succession planning) rather than for platform breadth, where AsureCentral spans payroll, HR, tax, benefits, recruiting, and time in one connected system. Overall Comparison Across All Platforms Provider Payroll Accuracy and Compliance HR Module Depth Benefits Integrations Onboarding Automation Pricing Transparency Implementation Time Asure (AsureCentral or AsureWorks) Strong Moderate Strong Moderate Not publicly disclosed Not publicly disclosed Gusto Strong Limited Moderate Moderate Strong Not publicly disclosed ADP Workforce Now Strong Strong Not publicly disclosed Moderate Limited Limited Paycor Moderate Moderate Not publicly disclosed Moderate Limited Not publicly disclosed Rippling Moderate Moderate Moderate Strong Limited Not publicly disclosed BambooHR Not publicly disclosed Strong Moderate Moderate Strong Not publicly disclosed Paylocity Not publicly disclosed Moderate Moderate Moderate Not publicly disclosed Not publicly disclosed Namely Not publicly disclosed Moderate Not publicly disclosed Moderate Not publicly disclosed Not publicly disclosed Justworks Not publicly disclosed Moderate Strong Moderate Not publicly disclosed Not publicly disclosed Platform by Platform Breakdown 1. Asure (AsureCentral and AsureWorks), Best for Employers Who Want to Choose How the Work Gets Done Best For: Growing SMB and lower-mid-market employers, roughly 10 to 500 employees, that want payroll, HR, benefits, and onboarding on one connected platform, whether they run it themselves or hand routine execution to a managed team. Delivery Model: AsureCentral is Asure's self-service platform. AsureWorks is Asure's managed-service alternative, running on that same underlying system, so a buyer can start self-managed and move to a managed model later without switching platforms. Starting Price: Both AsureCentral and AsureWorks are quote-based, requiring a sales conversation rather than listing public per-employee pricing. Native Onboarding: Yes. AsureCentral consolidates payroll processing, employee records, time tracking, benefits administration, and employee self-service in one login, and onboarding tasks run inside that same environment. HR and Benefits: AsureCentral's benefits administration tools let employees view, manage, and enroll in benefits, and you keep your own choice of benefits, broker, and retirement partners. Asure HR Compliance support helps employers track ACA reporting obligations as headcount approaches the IRS's 50-full-time-equivalent Applicable Large Employer threshold. Key Limitation: Neither AsureCentral nor AsureWorks publishes per-employee pricing publicly, so buyers comparing sticker price alone will need a sales conversation before they can benchmark total cost. AsureWorks provides accountable execution, not a guarantee against every compliance outcome, and statutory liability for the work always stays with the employer. Verdict: For a buyer who wants one platform but hasn't decided who should run it, Asure is one of the few entries on this list where that decision doesn't force a vendor switch later. AsureWorks also functions as a PEO alternative, since the client remains the employer of record and keeps its own choice of benefits, broker, and retirement partners, unlike a co-employment PEO model. 2. Gusto, Best for Small Businesses Wanting Simple Payroll and Benefits Best For: US small businesses, roughly two to 200 employees, running primarily single-state or lightly multi-state W-2 payroll, often through Gusto's accountant and bookkeeper channel. Starting Price: Gusto sells tiered subscription plans (Simple, Plus, Premium), each combining a monthly base fee with a per-person fee, plus separate pricing for Contractor Only and Gusto Global, its international-hiring product. Specific current dollar figures could not be independently confirmed on gusto.com this review cycle. Native Onboarding: Yes, per Gusto's own marketing, though an independent onboarding-automation benchmark was not available this cycle. HR Module: Gusto's HR tools center on core people records and benefits enrollment rather than deep workforce analytics. Key Limitation: Gusto is built for day-one simplicity. Buyers with heavier multi-state complexity or compliance-heavy operations often find it strongest early and thinner as the business scales. Verdict: Gusto rates well on this guide's pricing-transparency and simplicity criteria for straightforward, single-state-leaning payroll and benefits, particularly for buyers who want a tiered, publicly marketed pricing structure rather than a custom quote. 3. ADP Workforce Now, Best for Mid-Market Teams Wanting Broad Compliance Scale Best For: Employers roughly 50 to 999 employees that want a broad, multi-tier product line spanning RUN to enterprise HCM (adp.com), plus organizations that need international payroll reach through ADP's Global Payroll add-on. Starting Price: ADP Workforce Now is typically custom-quoted. Native Onboarding: ADP markets onboarding tools within its Workforce Now tier, though an independent automation-depth score was not confirmed this cycle. HR Module: ADP's HR tools span employee records, reporting, and compliance workflows across a product line that runs from small-business RUN to enterprise HCM. Its Global Payroll add-on, which integrates with Workforce Now, supports payroll in more than 140 countries and territories, according to ADP's own documentation, though that scope describes the global-payroll integration rather than a native Workforce Now specification. Key Limitation: ADP's custom-quote pricing model means buyers need a sales conversation before they can benchmark total cost, and rollout timelines vary based on company size and complexity. Verdict: ADP's advantage is scale and product-line breadth (adp.com) more than pricing transparency or fast rollout. 4. Paycor, Best for Mid-Market Teams Wanting Payroll and HR Analytics Together Best For: Mid-market employers, roughly 50 to 1,000 employees, looking for a packaged payroll and HR suite with reporting layered in. Starting Price: Paycor does not publish per-employee-per-month pricing. Its pricing page requires a sales conversation for a custom quote, according to Paycor's own site accessed July 10, 2026. Native Onboarding: Paycor includes onboarding workflows within its platform, though an independent automation-depth benchmark was not available this cycle. HR Module: An independent, sourced assessment of Paycor's HR module depth was not available this cycle. Key Limitation: The lack of public pricing means buyers cannot benchmark total cost without engaging sales. Verdict: Paycor suits a mid-market buyer prioritizing analytics alongside payroll, provided they're comfortable evaluating cost and support through a direct sales conversation rather than a public price list. 5. Rippling, Best for Fast-Growing Teams Wanting HR, IT, and Payroll in One Record Best For: SMB and mid-market employers, roughly 25 to 2,000 employees, that want to unify HR, payroll, benefits, and device or app provisioning under one employee record. Starting Price: Rippling's pricing is modular, built around a required core platform plus add-on modules, and is often quote-based. Specific per-employee-per-month figures could not be independently confirmed this cycle. Native Onboarding: Yes, spanning HR onboarding and IT provisioning together, according to Rippling's own marketing. HR Module: Rippling's HR tools are built around one employee record shared across payroll, IT, and device management, with a modular structure that lets employers add capabilities as they grow. Key Limitation: The modular pricing structure can make total cost difficult to estimate without scoping each module individually. Verdict: Rippling suits teams that want IT convergence alongside payroll and are prepared to scope modular pricing carefully. 6. BambooHR, Best for HR-First Teams Adding Payroll as a Secondary Need Best For: Employers that treat people management and HR records as the primary need, with payroll as a secondary, add-on priority. Starting Price: BambooHR publishes three per-employee-per-month tiers, Core at $10, Pro at $17, and Elite at $25, with a flat $250 monthly minimum for companies of 25 or fewer employees, according to BambooHR's own pricing page accessed July 10, 2026. Payroll itself is sold as a separate add-on whose price is not publicly listed, and a 15 percent discount applies when bundling payroll with benefits administration for US-based employees. Native Onboarding: BambooHR markets onboarding workflows as a core strength, though an independent automation benchmark was not confirmed this cycle. HR Module: BambooHR launched as a dedicated HR system before adding payroll, and its core plans center on employee records, org management, and people workflows. Key Limitation: Payroll is not included in the base HR plans, so a buyer treating payroll as a co-equal priority needs to price the add-on separately. G2 rating, benefits-carrier count, and implementation time were not independently confirmed for BambooHR this cycle. Verdict: BambooHR is one of the few providers on this list with genuinely public, per-employee pricing for its core HR plans, a real point in its favor for buyers who value pricing transparency, even though payroll pricing stays behind a sales call. 7. Paylocity, Best for Mid-Market Teams Prioritizing Benefits and Employee Engagement Best For: Mid-market employers, generally 100 to 1,000 employees, where benefits strategy and employee engagement sit alongside payroll as priorities. Starting Price: Paylocity's pricing is quote-based. Public per-employee rates could not be independently confirmed this cycle. Native Onboarding: Paylocity markets configurable onboarding workflows, though an independent automation-depth score was not available this cycle. HR Module: Paylocity is positioned in the market as a mid-market HCM platform with benefits administration and employee engagement tools alongside payroll and core HR. Key Limitation: G2 rating, benefits-carrier count, and implementation time were not independently confirmed for Paylocity this cycle, and the absence of public pricing means cost comparisons require a sales conversation. Verdict: Paylocity fits a mid-market buyer whose consolidation priority is benefits and engagement as much as payroll, though buyers should verify current pricing and carrier coverage directly before deciding. 8. Namely, Best for Mid-Market Teams Wanting a Branded Employee Experience Best For: Mid-market employers, roughly 50 to 500 employees, that prioritize a polished, branded, employee-facing HR experience alongside payroll. Starting Price: Namely's pricing is quote-based. A current, confirmed public pricing page could not be located for Namely this cycle. Native Onboarding: Namely markets a branded onboarding portal option, though an independent automation-depth benchmark was not available this cycle. HR Module: Namely is positioned in the market as an HR-first, mid-market platform built around employee self-service and a branded experience layer. Key Limitation: G2 rating, benefits-carrier count, implementation time, and payroll-compliance depth for complex multi-state scenarios were not independently confirmed for Namely this cycle; the comparison table above reflects that gap directly rather than an estimate. Verdict: Namely is worth a look for teams where HR brand and self-service adoption drive the decision, but compliance-heavy payroll needs may call for a more payroll-first evaluation alongside it. 9. Justworks, Best for Small Businesses Wanting PEO-Level Benefits Access Best For: Small businesses, generally under 100 employees, that want access to large-group benefits rates and are comfortable with a co-employment structure to get there. Starting Price: Justworks operates on a PEO pricing model. Current per-employee rates could not be independently confirmed this cycle. Native Onboarding: Justworks markets streamlined onboarding within its PEO model, though an independent automation-depth benchmark was not available this cycle. HR Module: Justworks bundles payroll, HR administration, and compliance support inside its PEO structure, with benefits access pooled across its client base. Key Limitation: As a PEO, Justworks becomes a co-employer of record alongside the client. Buyers who want to keep sole employer-of-record status and choose their own benefits, broker, or retirement partners will find that structure fundamentally different from a managed service such as AsureWorks, which involves no co-employment. G2 rating, benefits-carrier count, and implementation time were not independently confirmed for Justworks this cycle. Verdict: Justworks is the only PEO in this guide, and its case rests on pooled benefits access. Weigh that access against the co-employment tradeoff directly before deciding. Where Each Platform Shows a Documented Strength Support payroll accuracy and compliance most clearly through Gusto, ADP Workforce Now, and Asure, all three rated Strong on this criterion in the comparison table above; Asure's strength here reflects AsureCentral and AsureWorks' native multi-state tax filing, with Asure Payroll Tax Management available as additional specialized infrastructure Asure brings to more complex, higher-volume multi-jurisdiction cases. Show the clearest documented HR module depth through BambooHR and ADP Workforce Now, reflecting their histories as a dedicated HRIS and a broad HCM suite, respectively. Address benefits carrier integrations most directly through AsureCentral's benefits administration tools and Justworks's pooled PEO benefits access, though the two solve the problem in structurally different ways. One preserves the employer's own broker and carrier choices; the other pools access to group rates through co-employment. Rippling and Gusto market onboarding as a core strength, though independent onboarding benchmarks were not available this cycle. Publish the only confirmed, public per-employee pricing among the platforms in this guide through BambooHR and Gusto. Most of the rest, including Asure's AsureCentral and AsureWorks, ADP Workforce Now, Paycor, Rippling, Paylocity, and Namely, require a sales conversation to get a quote. Leave implementation time unconfirmed across every platform in this guide at a verified primary source this cycle. Treat any vendor or aggregator implementation-time claim as unconfirmed until you see it sourced directly. How to Choose Based on Your Company Size and Priority Company Size Primary Priority Consider Why 1 to 49 employees Fast, simple payroll and onboarding Gusto Publishes tiered pricing publicly and is built for straightforward, single-state-leaning payroll. AsureCentral is also quote-eligible at this size for buyers who want payroll, HR, and benefits in one login rather than a payroll-only tool. Under 100 employees Large-group benefits access Justworks PEO model pools benefits access, if co-employment fits your structure 10 to 250 employees One platform, undecided who runs it AsureCentral or AsureWorks Same underlying platform either way, so choosing self-managed or managed later does not require a switch 25 to 250 employees HR-first, payroll secondary BambooHR Built as a dedicated HR system with payroll and benefits available as add-ons 50 to 500 employees Growing compliance exposure near the 50-FTE threshold AsureCentral or AsureWorks with Asure HR Compliance AsureCentral's benefits administration tools and Asure HR Compliance support help track ACA and broader compliance obligations as headcount grows 50 to 1,000 employees HR analytics alongside payroll Paycor Packaged reporting and analytics layered on core payroll 100 to 1,000 employees Benefits strategy and employee engagement Paylocity Positioned in market around benefits administration and engagement tools 25 to 2,000 employees IT and HR convergence Rippling Unifies device and app provisioning with HR, benefits, and payroll 50 to 999 employees Multi-state compliance depth and product-line scale ADP Workforce Now Broad product-line scale spanning RUN to enterprise HCM, with Global Payroll reaching 140+ countries (adp.com, accessed July 10, 2026) Methodology and Sources This guide draws on two categories of information. The first is independently verified public data: the ACA's 50-full-time-equivalent Applicable Large Employer threshold (irs.gov, checked July 10, 2026), BambooHR's published pricing tiers (bamboohr.com, accessed July 10, 2026), ADP's Global Payroll country coverage (adp.com, accessed July 10, 2026), and Paycor's confirmed absence of public pricing (paycor.com, accessed July 10, 2026). The second is Asure's own qualitative analysis of publicly available vendor marketing and documented product scope, applied consistently across all nine entries and labeled Strong, Moderate, Limited, or Not publicly disclosed rather than scored on a numeric scale. Third-party review sentiment (G2, Capterra, and similar sources) was not used as an input to these labels, for any vendor, since that data could not be independently confirmed at a primary source (see below). Several figures commonly cited in payroll-provider comparisons could not be confirmed at a primary source during this review and were deliberately omitted rather than estimated: G2 or Capterra scores, review counts, benefits-carrier counts, and vendor-disclosed implementation times for Gusto, ADP, Paycor, Rippling, BambooHR, Paylocity, Namely, and Justworks; specific per-employee-per-month pricing for Gusto, Rippling, Namely, Paylocity, and Justworks; and any aggregate statistic describing how often SMBs using separate payroll and HR tools experience data-sync errors. Definitions for benefits administration, payroll processing, and employee onboarding automation, as used throughout this guide, follow the plain-language descriptions given under each criterion above. Frequently Asked Questions What does it mean for a payroll provider to be all in one? For this guide, an all-in-one payroll provider is one where payroll processing, core HR records, benefits enrollment, and new-hire onboarding automation all run inside a single login rather than through a separate onboarding tool or benefits broker portal that requires its own credentials and a manual data sync. AsureCentral, Gusto, ADP Workforce Now, Paycor, Rippling, BambooHR, Paylocity, and Namely all fit this definition to varying degrees; Justworks delivers similar scope through a PEO structure rather than a single-employer platform. Which payroll providers publish public per-employee pricing without a sales call? Of the platforms in this guide, BambooHR publishes the clearest tiered per-employee-per-month pricing on its own site, Core at $10, Pro at $17, and Elite at $25 (BambooHR, accessed July 10, 2026), and Gusto also markets tiered subscription pricing publicly. ADP Workforce Now, Paycor, Rippling, Paylocity, Namely, Justworks, and Asure's AsureCentral and AsureWorks all require a sales conversation for a specific quote, based on each provider's own pricing page as of this review. When does ACA compliance reporting start to apply as a company grows? Under the ACA's employer shared responsibility rules, a company becomes an Applicable Large Employer, subject to ACA reporting requirements, once it averages at least 50 full-time employees, including full-time-equivalent employees, in the prior calendar year (IRS, checked July 10, 2026). That threshold is a common trigger point for evaluating benefits-administration and compliance support, including AsureCentral's benefits administration tools and Asure HR Compliance support. Should I run payroll and HR myself, or have it managed for me? That depends on whether your team has the bandwidth and expertise to own payroll, tax filing, and HR administration day to day, or whether you'd rather keep decision authority while handing off routine execution. Asure supports both paths on one platform: AsureCentral for employers who want to run payroll and HR themselves, and AsureWorks for employers who want Asure specialists to handle the operational work, without the co-employment structure of a PEO. Is a PEO the same thing as a managed payroll service? No. A PEO, like Justworks, becomes a co-employer of record alongside the client and typically bundles benefits through its own pooled plans. A managed payroll service such as AsureWorks handles day-to-day payroll and HR execution, but the client remains the sole employer of record and keeps its own choice of benefits, broker, and retirement partners. Your Next Step If you've made it this far, you've probably already ruled out doing nothing. The remaining question is whether your team runs the new platform, or whether you'd rather have Asure's specialists run it for you while you stay the employer of record. AsureCentral gives you payroll, HR, benefits, time tracking, and onboarding in one login if you want to keep the work in-house. AsureWorks gives you the same platform with Asure specialists handling payroll, tax filing, and day-to-day HR administration if you'd rather redirect that time toward the business, without giving up control over your benefits or your people decisions. See how AsureCentral and AsureWorks compare side by side with the other providers in this guide before you sign anything. title: SeaWorld San Diego Debuts a One-of-a-Kind Wonder: Jewels of the Sea – The Ultimate Jellyfish Experience!
summary: SeaWorld San Diego Debuts a One-of-a-Kind Wonder: Jewels of the Sea – The Ultimate Jellyfish Experience! The largest standalone jellyfish exhibit in the country and a must-see in Southern California.
body_text: SAN DIEGO, CA (March 19, 2025) – – SeaWorld San Diego is thrilled to unveil its highly anticipated Jewels of the Sea: The Jellyfish Experience , the largest standalone jellyfish exhibit in the country, is now open to the public. Starting today, visitors are invited to immerse themselves in the mesmerizing world of jellyfish, in this groundbreaking, first-of-its-kind attraction at SeaWorld Parks. Jewels of the Sea showcases the enchanting beauty, fascinating biology, and mysterious allure of these otherworldly animals. Designed to be both captivating and educational, Jewels of the Sea offers visitors a unique opportunity to explore a variety of jellyfish species through engaging, interactive exhibits. The experience features three distinct galleries, each offering a unique perspective on jellyfish and showcasing the variety of jelly species and their locations from the shallow levels of ocean to the deep unknown. Guests begin their journey with an introduction to the fascinating world of jellies, answering key questions about their stings, life cycle, and anatomy. The murals on the walls will guide guests from shallow mangrove forests, where upside-down jellies live, through coral reefs, and into a deep ocean trench, symbolizing deeper exploration. The exhibit opens with nine unique varieties of jellies species displayed through over 15 aquariums. Highlights include one of the largest jellyfish cylinders in the country, a cascading water globe filled with jellyfish, and a fully interactive LED gallery that brings the wonders of the ocean to life. Throughout Jewels of the Sea, the wall corners are rounded to symbolize the flow of ocean currents. The lighting pulses from the arch to the cylinder tank, mimicking the movement of jellies in ocean currents. The exhibit provides a deep dive into the jellyfish life cycle, anatomy, and conservation – one of the key reasons SeaWorld San Diego chose to create this experience. The exhibit also underscores SeaWorld's commitment to marine education and the preservation of ocean ecosystems. In conjunction with the exhibit's grand opening and to highlight the crucial role that jellyfish play in understanding ocean health, SeaWorld partnered with Washed Ashore , a nonprofit organization dedicated to ocean conservation to present a powerful new art installation. Located just outside Jewels of the Sea, the life-sized Lion’s Mane Jellyfish sculpture, made entirely from upcycled marine debris, serves as a striking reminder of the devastating impact of plastic pollution on marine life. Crafted from discarded materials like ropes, plastic bottles, and foam buoys, the sculpture stands as a symbol of the urgent need to reduce waste and protect our oceans. "We’re thrilled to introduce Jewels of the Sea , a one-of-a-kind experience where guests can witness the breathtaking beauty of jellyfish like never before.” said Tyler Carter, Park President of SeaWorld San Diego. “This exhibit not only celebrates these captivating creatures but also highlights their critical role in ocean ecosystems. The Washed Ashore sculpture amplifies the message of ocean conservation and encourages all of us to reflect on how we can help reduce ocean pollution.” “Lion's Mane Jellies are the largest of jellyfish in the world, but their size can't prevent them from the impacts of ocean plastic pollution. Sea creatures of all sizes are being harmed when they mistake microplastics for food or become entangled in this marine debris,” said Brad Parks, Conservation Education Director, Washed Ashore. “We hope this sculpture and all the amazing animals at SeaWorld San Diego inspire every guest to do just one thing to help reduce plastic consumption and pollution, protecting wild places and the wildlife that depends on clean oceans to survive.” To further enhance the experience, SeaWorld is offering the exclusive Jelly Up-Close Tour. This behind-the-scenes journey provides guests with a closer look at SeaWorld’s jellyfish propagation program, along with an opportunity for hands-on interactions with these fascinating creatures in an educational setting.
